assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks improved frequency stability and accuracy by orders of magnitude, to the 1e-18 level, by trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength and interrogating them with ultra-stable lasers. This is exactly the measurement-limited progress I value: a new way of measuring that opens gravitational redshift sensing at the millimetre scale, geodesy, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and a redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye led the demonstration of the leading experimental systems with ultra-stable lasers, so a two-person prize is natural. Other contributors (e.g., Lemonde, Bloom/Ludlow, Hollberg-lineage groups) exist, but the supplied credit gives a clean, defensible pair.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups worldwide have reproduced and surpassed the original performance, and comparisons between clocks are routine; the 2005 prize covered the comb, and this is the natural follow-on. Timely and mature, although the redefinition of the second is not yet complete.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to credit a broader group of clock pioneers than the two supplied names.
Overlap with prior recognition of optical frequency combs and ion-trap clocks needs careful framing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms turned the interferometer into a precision instrument for gravity, rotation, the fine-structure constant and tests of the equivalence principle. It is a genuine new measurement technique, with field-deployable gravimeters and gradiometers, and potential for gravitational-wave detection and the geophysical applications I know are important.
assessment.attribution: Bordé laid out the theoretical and early experimental foundations of light-pulse atom interferometry, Pritchard developed the first atom interferometers with gratings and atomic beams, and Kasevich demonstrated precision gravimetry and gradiometry. The list also has Holger Müller, whose precision measurements are strong but more recent; I choose the three with the most decisive foundational contributions. Chu and Kasevich-lineage credit overlaps with an earlier prize in laser cooling.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed and reproduced across many laboratories over three decades and now commercial and field-deployed. Recognition is overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Allocation among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Müller and others (e.g., Chu, Mlynek, Kasevich-Chu collaboration) is genuinely contested.
The scale of the largest applications (large-baseline gravitational-wave or dark-matter detectors) is not yet realised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Controlled coherent interfaces between light and atomic ensembles or single atoms, including electromagnetically induced transparency, slow and stored light, quantum memories and cavity-QED photon-atom gates, underpin quantum networks and repeaters. This is close to my own field of quantum memories, and I know how hard efficiency, storage time and fidelity are in practice. The importance is real and the experimental demonstrations are careful.
assessment.attribution: Kimble (DLCZ-type networks, cavity QED, quantum state transfer), Rempe (single-atom cavity QED, photon-atom gates, single-photon sources) and Lukin (EIT-based storage and quantum interfaces) are leading candidates. I note that the field has many other decisive contributors (Hau and Harris on slow light, Lukin/Fleischhauer theory, Polzik, Gisin, rare-earth crystal groups), so the compound discovery risks leaving out parts of the credit.
assessment.maturity: The demonstrations are confirmed in many platforms, but deployed quantum networks and repeaters have not yet shown a decisive advantage. The field is advancing but the final practical impact is not yet settled.
uncertainties: The discovery is a compound of several platforms, and fair attribution between atom-cavity, ensemble and solid-state memories is unresolved.
Practical network performance and scalability remain to be proven.
I have a possible bias as someone working on rare-earth-crystal memories.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED supplies the architecture for strong coupling, dispersive readout and control of superconducting qubits, and is the working basis for most superconducting quantum processors. It enabled quantum non-demolition measurement, error-correction experiments and quantum-limited amplification chains. Impact on other work is very high.
assessment.attribution: Blais proposed the circuit QED theory, Wallraff demonstrated strong coupling in the first experiment with Schoelkopf's group, and Schoelkopf's group followed up with the transmon-based cQED architecture and bosonic codes. The credit among these three is reasonably clear, with some overlap with Devoret and others recognised in 2025.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and extended across all superconducting platforms; mature. However, the 2025 prize to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes the timing and overlap questionable.
uncertainties: Overlap with the recent 2025 superconducting-circuit prize and whether the committee feels the area was just recognised.
Whether the Nobel scope should reflect the architecture (applied engineering) or the underlying physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade in optical-tweezer arrays enables programmable many-body quantum simulation and high-fidelity gates with hundreds of atoms. It combines established atomic physics (blockade, tweezers) with a rapid expansion into quantum simulators and processors, and the experimental control achieved is impressive.
assessment.attribution: Saffman and Zoller's early blockade gate proposals, Browaeys's and Lukin's tweezer-array demonstrations, and Lukin's programmable simulators are central. Jaksch and Zoller proposals and Weiss, Regal, Ahn and Endres groups also contributed, so I am concerned that three names may leave out decisive people.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing but still developing; error rates, scalability and the long-term role of neutral atoms against competing platforms are open. The prize may be somewhat premature compared with older candidates.
uncertainties: Contested allocation between theory proposers (Jaksch, Zoller) and tweezer-array experimenters.
Premature relative to the final shape of the field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light for interferometry demonstrates how quantum noise limits can be beaten in practice, now in gravitational-wave detectors where squeezing improves the observable event rate. This is a clear case of a quantum technique extending the measurement frontier, which I value strongly.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the theoretical proposal for squeezed-state interferometry, Kimble's group generated squeezing experimentally (with Slusher at Bell Labs as an essential early experimentalist not listed), and Schnabel and others developed the practical sources used in GEO600 and LIGO. The list omits major figures, so a fair three-person configuration is hard.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by routine operation in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600. The impact on a recent Nobel-recognised field (gravitational waves, 2017) adds context and maturity.
uncertainties: Slusher and Walls/Yurke-lineage contributions are not among the credited names, which limits a fair configuration.
Frequency-dependent squeezing and the Nobel scale versus an enabling technology.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, giving quantum gas microscopes, Mott insulators and a route to quantum simulation. It is a new way of observing many-body physics with single-site resolution, valuable for both measurement and understanding.
assessment.attribution: Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger delivered decisive experiments (Mott transition, Fermi-Hubbard, quantum gas microscope), while Jaksch, Zoller and Cirac provided the theory. The list contains five names, so a three-person prize needs a theory/experiment choice; I pick experimental leaders.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and reproduced in many laboratories; mature. Part of the field overlaps with the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems.
uncertainties: Choice between experimentalists and theorists (Cirac, Zoller) is contentious.
Whether quantum simulation has yet produced results beyond classical reach.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Aberration-corrected electron microscopy brought sub-angstrom resolution to routine imaging, allowing direct imaging of atoms and defects in materials. It is a clear instrument-and-method advance that opened new ways of observing matter, similar in spirit to earlier Nobel-recognised instruments such as the electron microscope and STM.
assessment.attribution: Rose supplied the theoretical design of the corrector, Haider and Urban built and demonstrated the working correctors in practice. This trio is a coherent, well-known credit set, with Krivanek as a notable contender not among the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Mature and in widespread use for two decades. Recognition is timely or overdue, and applications in materials, catalysis and 2D materials are extensive.
uncertainties: Krivanek (Nion) and others made independent decisive contributions that are not in the credited set.
Debate on whether the work counts as physics rather than instrumentation or chemistry.
